new.caption:
Payday. Where should the money go first? Follow this order.

1. A safety net: one month of bills in savings, then build toward 3 to 6 months.
2. If your employer matches retirement savings, put in enough to get the full match. Skip it and you leave part of your pay on the table.
3. Then invest in your TFSA, in a low-fee index fund, and leave it alone.

Why this order: the safety net keeps a surprise bill off your credit card. The match only pays if you put money in. Then time does the rest.

The catch: carrying card debt at 20% or more? Paying it down usually comes before step 3.

Do this: this payday, set up one automatic transfer to stop 1. Add the others as you go.

Not guaranteed. Returns vary. Education, not advice.

Follow for one money move a day, in plain words.

#personalfinancecanada #payday #tfsa #emergencyfund #moneytips

new.caption:
Not married? No will? In Ontario, your partner may get nothing.

If you die without a will in Ontario, the law decides who inherits:
Married spouse: everything if the estate is under $350,000; otherwise the first $350,000, and the rest is shared with your children.
Common-law partner: nothing under these rules, even after years together. They may have to go to court to ask for support.

The fix is one will. It says who gets what, and who you'd want to raise your kids.

Do this: this week, book one call with a wills lawyer and ask, "What does a will and power of attorney cost for both of us?"

Other provinces have different rules, so check yours.

Send this to your partner.

Follow for one money move a day, in plain words.

#wills #estateplanning #commonlaw #personalfinancecanada #moneyfoundations
new.first_comment: Sources: Steps to Justice (CLEO, Community Legal Education Ontario), 'Learn what happens to your property if you die without a will' (stepstojustice.ca): a married spouse gets everything if the estate is under $350,000, otherwise the first $350,000 (deaths on or after March 1, 2021) and the rest is shared with the children; the intestacy rules leave nothing to a common-law partner, who may be able to make a dependant's support claim in court. Ontario Succession Law Reform Act, R.S.O. 1990, c. S.26, Part II (intestacy) and Part V (dependants' support), ontario.ca/laws. Rules differ by province. General information, not legal advice.

new.caption:
Putting TFSA money back? Wait. Here's the trap.

You take out $5,000 in March and put it back in June. Feels harmless. But the room from a withdrawal only comes back on January 1 of the next year. If you had no other room left, that $5,000 is an over-contribution, and the CRA charges 1% a month on it until it's out: $50 a month, about $350 from June to December.

Do this: before you put money back, check your room in CRA My Account (it shows your room as of January 1). Moving money between banks? Ask for a direct transfer, which doesn't count as a withdrawal.

Already did it? Take the extra out as soon as you can, and look up form RC243 (the TFSA return) on canada.ca.

The rule to remember: out this year? Back in January.

Send this to your TFSA friend.

Follow for one money move a day, in plain words.

#TFSA #personalfinancecanada #CRA #taxtips #moneyfoundations
new.first_comment: Sources: CRA (canada.ca), 'Before you contribute to a TFSA' and the TFSA withdrawal pages: withdrawals are added back to your contribution room at the beginning of the following year; an excess amount is taxed 1% per month for each month it stays in the account; direct transfers between your own TFSAs are not withdrawals; excess amounts are reported on form RC243. Your room as of January 1 is in CRA My Account (subtract this year's deposits). Maths: 1% of $5,000 = $50 for each month the excess stays in; June through December = 7 months = $350. Education, not tax advice.

new.caption:
Paid Friday. Broke by Wednesday? The habit: pay yourself first.

Rich Habits, Decoded No. 1. Each episode takes one money habit and shows you how to do it on a normal paycheque.

WHAT IT MEANS: savings come out the day your pay lands, automatically, before you can spend it. You live on what's left, instead of saving what's left.

WHY IT WORKS: you don't rely on willpower. In the 'Save More Tomorrow' study, workers who signed up to save automatically, with the rate rising at each raise, went from saving 3.5% of pay to 13.6% over 40 months.

HOW TO DO IT (10 minutes in your banking app):
1. Open a separate savings account (ideally one that pays interest and that you don't see every day).
2. Set an automatic transfer for payday. Start at 10%; if that's too much, start at 1% or 2%.
3. Every raise: add 1 percentage point.
4. Leave it. The point is not having to decide again.

THE CATCH: if you carry card debt at 20%+, point the automatic payment at that first. Keep a small buffer so the transfer never bounces.

Do this: set one automatic transfer for your next payday, even if it's $10.

Rich Habits, Decoded No. 2 is Wednesday at 5 pm.

Education only, not financial advice.

Follow for one money move a day, in plain words.
